messages.author: 194004d81259bcfd
messages.subject: genotype call question
parts:
Hi,

I have a question which is not directly related to aroma but there
should be experts here. For Hapmap SNP genotypes estimated from Affy
SNP arrays (e.g. 500K), if a SNP actually only has 1 copy of A, will
it be called as genotype AA? Similarly, if a person has 3 copies of A,
will it still be called as AA? What if this person has AAB....will it
be called as AB? I ask this because there are only 4 types of
genotypes I can see in the Hapmap database (AA, AB, BB, NN) so I
wonder what happens if a SNP is not a dipolid.

Thanks!
Yu Chuan

> should be experts here. For Hapmap SNP genotypes estimated from Affy
> SNP arrays (e.g. 500K), if a SNP actually only has 1 copy of A, will
> it be called as genotype AA? Similarly, if a person has 3 copies of A,
> will it still be called as AA? What if this person has AAB....will it
> be called as AB? I ask this because there are only 4 types of
> genotypes I can see in the Hapmap database (AA, AB, BB, NN) so I
> wonder what happens if a SNP is not a dipolid.

To the best of my understanding, the HapMap genotype calls have been
done using methods that assume two copies and that ignore the fact
that copy-number aberrations may occur. So, yes, single-copy A and B
have most likely been called AA and AB (or AB or NN), and so on.

/Henrik

>
> Thanks!
> Yu Chuan

messages.author: 185f4d4fdb048fb8
messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] Re: genotype call question
parts:
Genotyping algorithms classify, typically two-dimensional, data points
into three groups AA, AB, and BB. Some methods also call data points
NoCall, but not all. What a particular data points is classified
depends on where the classification boundaries are.

For methods like RLMM and CRLMM that classify data in a (thetaA,
thetaB) space it is likely that data points "outside" the AA-AB-BB
region will call it AA, AB, or BB, but probably not NoCall because
that often corresponds to a too weak signal. It is also likely that
an A is called AA, but due to noise it might be called AB, less likely
B though. But, yes, it is reasonable to assume that the more A:s
there is relative to B:s, the more likely it is to be called AA.

/H
